title: SQL Day 1 — SELECT & Reading Business Data
description: Build the foundation for retrieving and presenting business data with SELECT.

topics.title: SELECT — Retrieving Business Data
topics.business_skill: Retrieve required fields from a business table.

teaching.teacher:
# SQL SELECT
SELECT is the starting point for analytical SQL. It tells the database which fields the analyst wants returned.

Basic pattern:
SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name;

Start by translating the manager's request into the exact fields required.
teaching.explain: SELECT chooses the columns you want to see. FROM identifies the table containing them.
teaching.detailedlearning: Avoid SELECT * when a report only needs a few fields. Explicit columns make the result easier to validate, document, and maintain.
teaching.expose: Think in two questions: Where is the data? Which fields does the stakeholder need?
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, customer_name, sales FROM orders;
teaching.business_question: The sales manager needs a transaction review showing the order ID, customer name, sales, and profit. Return only those fields.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, customer_name, sales, profit FROM orders;

questions.scenario: The manager is reviewing this week's transactions.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, and sales.
questions.validation: Return exactly the requested columns from orders.

questions.request: Return order ID, sales, profit, and discount.

questions.scenario: A regional review requires customer, product, geography, and financial fields.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, product name, region, sales, and profit.
questions.validation: Return exactly the six requested fields.

topics.title: Selecting Multiple Columns
topics.business_skill: Assemble a useful analytical view from several fields.

teaching.teacher:
## Multiple columns
Separate requested columns with commas. The order you specify is the order returned.
teaching.explain: SELECT can return one field or many fields.
teaching.detailedlearning: Column selection should follow the stakeholder's reporting requirement. Do not add unrelated fields merely because they exist.
teaching.expose: Treat the SELECT list as the output contract.
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, category, sales, profit FROM orders;
teaching.business_question: The category manager wants a product-performance view containing product name, category, quantity, sales, and profit.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT product_name, category, quantity, sales, profit FROM orders;

questions.scenario: The manager wants a category performance snapshot.

questions.request: Return order ID, order date, ship mode, and region.

questions.scenario: Leadership wants a compact transaction view for commercial review.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, category, sales, discount, profit, and region.
questions.validation: Return all seven requested fields in the requested order.

teaching.teacher:
## Aliases
Use AS to rename a returned column without changing the source data.

Example:
SELECT sales AS total_sales FROM orders;
teaching.explain: An alias changes the label shown in the result.
teaching.detailedlearning: Aliases improve report readability. Use stable snake_case or clear business labels depending on the platform contract.
teaching.expose: Separate source field names from presentation names. The database column stays unchanged.
teaching.example: SELECT sales AS revenue, profit AS gross_profit FROM orders;
teaching.business_question: Finance wants the result labels to clearly identify sales as Revenue and profit as Profit.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT sales AS Revenue, profit AS Profit FROM orders;

questions.scenario: Finance wants a cleaner report header.
questions.request: Return sales as Revenue and profit as Profit.
questions.validation: Use aliases for the requested result labels.

questions.scenario: A dashboard dataset requires consistent field names.
questions.request: Return order ID as Order_ID and customer name as Customer.
questions.validation: Use aliases matching the requested names.

questions.scenario: The BI layer needs semantic names for transaction metrics.
questions.request: Return sales as Total_Sales, quantity as Units, and discount as Discount_Rate.
questions.validation: Use aliases for all three measures.

topics.title: Calculated Columns in SELECT
topics.business_skill: Create simple analytical values directly in a query.

teaching.teacher:
## Calculated expressions
SQL can calculate values while returning rows.

Example:
SELECT sales - profit AS estimated_cost FROM orders;

The source data is not changed.
teaching.explain: An expression combines columns or constants to produce a new result.
teaching.detailedlearning: Calculated fields are useful for quick analysis. Always define what the calculation represents before using it in a business decision.
teaching.expose: Ask: What business metric can be derived from the available fields?
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, sales - profit AS estimated_cost FROM orders;
teaching.business_question: The finance analyst wants an estimated non-profit portion of each order using sales minus profit.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, sales, profit, sales - profit AS estimated_cost FROM orders;

questions.scenario: Finance wants to see the portion of sales not represented by profit.
questions.request: Return order ID and sales minus profit as Estimated_Cost.
questions.validation: Calculate sales - profit and alias it Estimated_Cost.

questions.scenario: Management wants to compare order economics.
questions.request: Return order ID, sales, profit, and profit as a percentage of sales.
questions.validation: Calculate profit / sales and expose it as Profit_Margin.

questions.scenario: A margin review needs a derived discount impact indicator.
questions.request: Return order ID, sales, discount, and sales multiplied by discount as Discount_Amount.
questions.validation: Calculate sales * discount and alias it Discount_Amount.

topics.title: Building a Business Output
topics.business_skill: Translate a stakeholder request into a complete SELECT query.

teaching.teacher:
## From request to query
A production analyst starts with the required output, identifies the table, selects fields, then adds calculations or aliases only where needed.
teaching.explain: A good SELECT query directly reflects the business request.
teaching.detailedlearning: Before executing, verify table, fields, calculations, labels, and output order. This becomes the foundation for later WHERE, GROUP BY, JOIN, and window analysis.
teaching.expose: SQL is a translation layer between business language and data structures.
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, customer_name, sales, profit, sales - profit AS estimated_cost FROM orders;
teaching.business_question: A senior analyst is preparing a transaction-level profitability extract. Return order ID, customer, category, sales, profit, and estimated cost (sales minus profit).
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, customer_name, category, sales, profit, sales - profit AS estimated_cost FROM orders;

questions.scenario: The manager needs a transaction list for a morning review.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, category, sales, and profit.

questions.scenario: Finance needs an order-level profitability extract.
questions.request: Return order ID, sales, profit, and sales minus profit as Estimated_Cost.
questions.validation: Include the requested calculation and alias.

questions.scenario: Leadership needs a compact commercial extract for downstream reporting.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer, category, region, sales, profit, and profit/sales as Profit_Margin.
questions.validation: Return all requested fields and calculate profit divided by sales.
